items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "irreversible".
items.answer: Cannot easily be changed back to the starting substances
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: cannot easily be changed back to the starting substances. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between effervescence and boiling.
items.answer: Effervescence is bubbles of a gas produced by a reaction (e.g. CO₂ from acid and carbonate); boiling is bubbles of the liquid’s own vapour forming when it is heated to its boiling point.
items.markingKey: Effervescence is bubbles of a gas produced by a reaction (e.g. CO₂ from acid and carbonate); boiling is bubbles of the liquid’s own vapour forming when it is heated to its boiling point. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why dissolving salt in water is a physical change.
items.answer: No new substance is made; the salt can be recovered by evaporating the water. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: No new substance is made; the salt can be recovered by evaporating the water. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to The Statue of Liberty’s green colour, explain how it illustrates a slow chemical change.
items.answer: The copper skin of the statue was originally shiny brown; over about 30 years it reacted with oxygen, water and carbon dioxide in the air to form a green patina. The patina protects the copper underneath from further corrosion.
items.markingKey: Context (The copper skin of the statue was originally shiny brown; over about 30 years it reacted with oxygen, water and carbon dioxide in the air to form a green patina.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The patina protects the copper underneath from further corrosion. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a slow chemical change.

items.stem: A student claims: "If something changes colour it must be a chemical reaction." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Colour change is a common sign, but physical changes (e.g. dissolving coloured crystals or heating iron until it glows) can also change colour.
items.markingKey: Colour change is a common sign, but physical changes (e.g. dissolving coloured crystals or heating iron until it glows) can also change colour. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Cooking is mainly chemistry."
items.answer: Cooking combines physical and chemical changes; much of its flavour comes from chemical reactions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: browning, baking and caramelising are chemical reactions that make new flavours; raising agents produce CO₂ by reactions. Arguments against: melting butter, boiling water and dissolving sugar are physical changes. Supported judgement: Cooking combines physical and chemical changes; much of its flavour comes from chemical reactions.

items.stem: Which is a physical change?
items.answer: Chocolate melting
items.markingKey: D. It can be reversed by cooling.

items.stem: "Physical changes can never be reversed." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Physical changes such as melting, freezing and dissolving are usually easy to reverse.
items.markingKey: Physical changes such as melting, freezing and dissolving are usually easy to reverse. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Aiko plans to investigate how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the time for a marble chip to stop fizzing. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: volume of acid (25 cm³); mass and size of marble chip; temperature; swirling
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: volume of acid (25 cm³) – more acid reacts longer; mass and size of marble chip – surface area affects rate; temperature – heat speeds reactions; swirling – mixing affects rate. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: Arjun plans an investigation into how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the time for a marble chip to stop fizzing. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (concentration of hydrochloric acid (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 mol/dm³)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: When magnesium burns in air, why does the mass of the solid increase?
options: Oxygen from the air combines with the magnesium
items.answer: Oxygen from the air combines with the magnesium
items.markingKey: C. Product: magnesium oxide.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a closed system and an open system.
items.answer: In an open system gases can escape or be taken in, so mass may appear to change; in a closed system nothing escapes, so mass is constant.
items.markingKey: In an open system gases can escape or be taken in, so mass may appear to change; in a closed system nothing escapes, so mass is constant. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Complete the word equation: iron + sulfur → ?
items.answer: iron sulfide
items.markingKey: 1-2 iron sulfide (1 mark per correct product).

items.stem: Briefly describe Antoine Lavoisier (1770s) and explain what it reveals about law of conservation of mass.
items.answer: Lavoisier carefully weighed reactants and products in sealed vessels and showed that mass is conserved; he also showed that burning is a reaction with oxygen. His careful measurements helped turn chemistry into a quantitative science.
items.markingKey: Context (Lavoisier carefully weighed reactants and products in sealed vessels and showed that mass is conserved; he also showed that burning is a reaction with oxygen.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: His careful measurements helped turn chemistry into a quantitative science. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to law of conservation of mass.

items.stem: 40.0 g of lead nitrate solution is mixed with 20.0 g of potassium iodide solution in a beaker on a balance. A yellow precipitate forms. Predict the total mass after mixing and explain.
items.answer: 60.0 g; no gas is produced and atoms are only rearranged, so mass is conserved
items.markingKey: 1 60.0 g; 1 no substance escapes / atoms rearranged, not created or destroyed.

items.stem:
Aiko heated copper carbonate in an open tube and recorded the mass of solid remaining after different heating times.

Heating time / min | Mass of solid / g: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 4.92 | 4.79 | 4.86
2 | 4.08 | 4.05 | 3.97
4 | 2.28 | 3.51 | 3.40
6 | 3.29 | 3.22 | 3.21
8 | 3.14 | 3.21 | 3.23

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean mass of solid at 4 min, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 2.28 g (trial 1 at 4 min); mean = 3.46 g
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (2.28) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 3.46 g.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Lavoisier’s method of weighing everything in sealed vessels was the most important step in modern chemistry."
items.answer: It was one of several crucial steps; precise measurement made later theories possible.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: led to the law of conservation of mass and the end of phlogiston theory; made chemistry quantitative. Arguments against: other advances such as atomic theory and the periodic table were also essential. Supported judgement: It was one of several crucial steps; precise measurement made later theories possible.

items.stem: Sofia plans an investigation into whether mass is conserved when sodium hydrogencarbonate reacts with vinegar in an open and a sealed container. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (type of container (open flask or flask sealed with a balloon)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Explain why a reaction must be done in a sealed container to show conservation of mass when a gas is produced.
items.answer: Otherwise the gas escapes and its mass is not measured, so the products appear lighter.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Otherwise the gas escapes and its mass is not measured, so the products appear lighter. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Mass is lost when wood burns because the ash is lighter." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The missing mass is in the gases (CO₂ and water vapour) that escape; including them, mass is conserved.
items.markingKey: The missing mass is in the gases (CO₂ and water vapour) that escape; including them, mass is conserved. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Nia wants to find out whether mass is conserved when sodium hydrogencarbonate reacts with vinegar in an open and a sealed container. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does type of container affect change in total mass?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (type of container (open flask or flask sealed with a balloon)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (change in total mass measured on a balance (to 0.01 g)) in a question form.

items.stem: A flask containing acid and marble chips had a mass of 160.5 g at the start. With no bung, the mass after the reaction was 159.4 g. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced and explain why the mass fell.
items.answer: 1.1 g; the CO₂ gas escaped from the open flask (mass is still conserved)
items.markingKey: M1 160.5 − 159.4; A1 1.1 g; B1 gas escaped – atoms not destroyed.

items.stem: Which gas is produced by the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate?
items.answer: Carbon dioxide
items.markingKey: B. Calcium oxide is also formed.

items.stem: Distinguish between thermal decomposition and combustion.
items.answer: Thermal decomposition breaks one compound into simpler substances using heat, without needing oxygen; combustion is a reaction of a fuel with oxygen that releases energy.
items.markingKey: Thermal decomposition breaks one compound into simpler substances using heat, without needing oxygen; combustion is a reaction of a fuel with oxygen that releases energy. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why gas boilers need to be serviced regularly.
items.answer: A faulty boiler may have too little oxygen, causing incomplete combustion that produces toxic carbon monoxide. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A faulty boiler may have too little oxygen, causing incomplete combustion that produces toxic carbon monoxide. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: When 20 g of calcium carbonate is heated strongly, 11.2 g of calcium oxide is left. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide given off and write the word equation.
items.answer: 8.8 g; calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide
items.markingKey: M1 20 − 11.2; A1 8.8 g; B1 word equation.

items.stem: Kwame is investigating how the type of metal carbonate affects how quickly it thermally decomposes. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If copper carbonate is heated, then the limewater will go milky fastest, because carbonates of less reactive metals decompose more easily.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If copper carbonate is heated, then the limewater will go milky fastest, because carbonates of less reactive metals decompose more easily.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the type of metal carbonate affects how quickly it thermally decomposes. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): suck-back can crack hot glass – remove the delivery tube first; wear eye protection. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. suck-back can crack hot glass – remove the delivery tube first; wear eye protection); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "fuel"?
options: A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature falls
A reaction in which a substance burns in oxygen, releasing energy as heat and light
A substance that releases energy when it burns
A change in which new substances are formed and which is usually hard to reverse
items.answer: A substance that releases energy when it burns
items.markingKey: C. "fuel" is a substance that releases energy when it burns.

items.stem: A student claims: "Oxygen is a fuel." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Oxygen is needed for burning, but it is not a fuel; the fuel is the substance that reacts with oxygen and releases energy.
items.markingKey: Oxygen is needed for burning, but it is not a fuel; the fuel is the substance that reacts with oxygen and releases energy. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Nia burned different volumes of ethanol in a spirit burner under a can of water and recorded the temperature rise.

Volume of ethanol burned / cm³ | Temperature rise / °C: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 9.8 | 10.1 | 9.9
2 | 13.4 | 19.6 | 20.8
3 | 31.1 | 30.0 | 30.1
4 | 40.3 | 41.7 | 41.1
5 | 52.2 | 50.8 | 50.2

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean temperature rise at 2 cm³, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 13.4 °C (trial 1 at 2 cm³); mean = 20.20 °C
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (13.4) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 20.20 °C.

items.stem: Describe how you could show that the products of burning a candle include water and carbon dioxide, and explain what happens if the air supply is reduced.
items.answer: Draw combustion products from a burning candle through a cooled U-tube (water condenses – test with blue cobalt chloride paper turning pink or anhydrous copper sulfate turning blue), then through limewater (turns milky – CO₂). With less air: incomplete combustion – yellow sooty flame, carbon (soot) and toxic carbon monoxide form, less energy released.
items.markingKey: Draw combustion products from a burning candle through a cooled U-tube (water condenses – test with blue cobalt chloride paper turning pink or anhydrous copper sulfate turning blue), then through limewater (turns milky – CO₂). With less air: incomplete combustion – yellow sooty flame, carbon (soot) and toxic carbon monoxide form, less energy released.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A device using an exothermic reaction (often iron oxidation) to release heat"?
items.answer: hand warmer
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of hand warmer.

items.stem: Hana writes: "All reactions that need heating are endothermic." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Many exothermic reactions (e.g. burning) need heat to start; the overall energy change decides the type.
items.markingKey: Many exothermic reactions (e.g. burning) need heat to start; the overall energy change decides the type. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a match needs to be struck before it burns even though combustion is exothermic.
items.answer: Energy is needed to start the reaction (activation energy); once started, the energy released keeps it going.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Energy is needed to start the reaction (activation energy); once started, the energy released keeps it going. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Zara plans to investigate how the mass of ammonium nitrate dissolved affects the temperature drop of the water. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: volume of water (25 cm³); starting temperature; stirring; polystyrene cup
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: volume of water (25 cm³) – larger volume cools less; starting temperature – affects heat gained from surroundings; stirring – ensures it dissolves fully; polystyrene cup – insulation reduces heat transfer. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

Sana added different masses of calcium oxide to 50 cm³ of water in a polystyrene cup and recorded the temperature rise.

items.answer: 4 g; range = 1.1 °C; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 4 g; 1 range = max − min = 20.2 − 19.1 = 1.1 °C; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Hana plans an investigation into how the mass of ammonium nitrate dissolved affects the temperature drop of the water. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (mass of ammonium nitrate (1, 2, 3, 4, 5 g)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "exothermic reaction".
items.answer: A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature rises
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature rises. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an endothermic change such as thermal decomposition and an exothermic change such as burning.
items.answer: An exothermic reaction gives out energy and the temperature rises (e.g. burning); an endothermic reaction takes in energy and the temperature falls (e.g. thermal decomposition).
items.markingKey: An exothermic reaction gives out energy and the temperature rises (e.g. burning); an endothermic reaction takes in energy and the temperature falls (e.g. thermal decomposition). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The temperature of a solution changed from 20.0 °C to 13.5 °C during a reaction. Calculate the temperature change and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: -6.5 °C; endothermic
items.markingKey: M1 13.5 − 20.0; A1 -6.5 °C; B1 endothermic – energy taken in from surroundings.

items.stem: Plan an investigation to find whether dissolving different salts is exothermic or endothermic, and explain how you would show the results.
items.answer: Measure 25 cm³ water in a polystyrene cup (insulation); record start temperature; add 5 g salt, stir; record lowest or highest temperature; calculate change; repeat three times per salt; keep volume, mass, starting temperature the same; rise → exothermic, fall → endothermic; display as a bar chart of temperature change.
items.markingKey: Measure 25 cm³ water in a polystyrene cup (insulation); record start temperature; add 5 g salt, stir; record lowest or highest temperature; calculate change; repeat three times per salt; keep volume, mass, starting temperature the same; rise → exothermic, fall → endothermic; display as a bar chart of temperature change.

items.stem: Which metal does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid?
items.answer: Copper
items.markingKey: B. It is below hydrogen.

items.stem: Briefly explain why potassium is stored under oil.
items.answer: It reacts rapidly with oxygen and water vapour in the air; oil keeps air and water away.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It reacts rapidly with oxygen and water vapour in the air; oil keeps air and water away. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which Galvanised steel and sacrificial protection shows using reactivity to prevent corrosion.
items.answer: Steel is coated with zinc; because zinc is more reactive, it corrodes instead of the iron even if the coating is scratched. Used for car bodies, lamp posts and ships’ hulls (with zinc or magnesium blocks).
items.markingKey: Context (Steel is coated with zinc; because zinc is more reactive, it corrodes instead of the iron even if the coating is scratched.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Used for car bodies, lamp posts and ships’ hulls (with zinc or magnesium blocks). – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to using reactivity to prevent corrosion.

items.stem: Sofia plans to investigate how the reactivity of a metal affects the temperature rise when it reacts with hydrochloric acid. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: mass of metal (0.5 g powder); volume and concentration of acid; starting temperature; insulated cup
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: mass of metal (0.5 g powder) – more metal releases more energy; volume and concentration of acid – both affect the amount reacting; starting temperature – affects rate; insulated cup – reduces heat loss. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Coating steel with zinc is the best way to prevent bridges from rusting."
items.answer: Galvanising is excellent for many steel parts but engineers compare costs and conditions to choose the best protection.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: protects even when scratched (sacrificial); long-lasting. Arguments against: costly for large structures; paint or stainless steel may be cheaper or more suitable; zinc slowly wears away. Supported judgement: Galvanising is excellent for many steel parts but engineers compare costs and conditions to choose the best protection.

items.stem: A piece of zinc is placed in magnesium sulfate solution. Will a displacement reaction happen?
options: No – zinc is less reactive than magnesium
No – metals never react with salt solutions
Yes – zinc is more reactive than magnesium, so it displaces magnesium
Yes – all metals displace each other
items.answer: No – zinc is less reactive than magnesium
items.markingKey: A. B1 No – zinc is less reactive than magnesium

items.stem: Ana writes: "All metals react with acids to make hydrogen." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Metals below hydrogen in the reactivity series, such as copper, silver and gold, do not react with dilute acids.
items.markingKey: Metals below hydrogen in the reactivity series, such as copper, silver and gold, do not react with dilute acids. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Kwame investigated how the reactivity of a metal affects the temperature rise when it reacts with hydrochloric acid. The method had this weakness: metal ribbon was used for magnesium but lumps for iron. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: use powder of all metals so that surface area is similar
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: use powder of all metals so that surface area is similar

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "balanced equation".
items.answer: A symbol equation with the same number of each type of atom on both sides
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a symbol equation with the same number of each type of atom on both sides. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Fizzing caused by a gas being produced in a reaction"?
items.answer: effervescence
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of effervescence.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "thermal decomposition".
items.answer: The breaking down of a compound into simpler substances by heating
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the breaking down of a compound into simpler substances by heating. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between an endothermic change such as thermal decomposition and an exothermic change such as burning.
items.answer: An exothermic reaction gives out energy and the temperature rises (e.g. burning); an endothermic reaction takes in energy and the temperature falls (e.g. thermal decomposition).
items.markingKey: An exothermic reaction gives out energy and the temperature rises (e.g. burning); an endothermic reaction takes in energy and the temperature falls (e.g. thermal decomposition). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a reactive metal and an unreactive metal.
items.answer: A reactive metal (e.g. potassium) reacts quickly with water, oxygen and acids; an unreactive metal (e.g. gold) barely reacts and is found native.
items.markingKey: A reactive metal (e.g. potassium) reacts quickly with water, oxygen and acids; an unreactive metal (e.g. gold) barely reacts and is found native. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Complete the word equation: methane + oxygen → ?
items.answer: carbon dioxide + water
items.markingKey: 1-2 carbon dioxide + water (1 mark per correct product).

items.stem: Distinguish between a physical change and a chemical change.
items.answer: A physical change makes no new substance and is usually reversible (e.g. melting); a chemical change makes new substances and is usually hard to reverse (e.g. burning).
items.markingKey: A physical change makes no new substance and is usually reversible (e.g. melting); a chemical change makes new substances and is usually hard to reverse (e.g. burning). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why water should not be used on an oil or electrical fire.
items.answer: Water sinks below burning oil and boils violently, spreading the fire; water conducts electricity and can cause electrocution.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Water sinks below burning oil and boils violently, spreading the fire; water conducts electricity and can cause electrocution. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Endothermic reactions make things colder because they produce cold." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: They take in thermal energy from the surroundings; “cold” is not a substance.
items.markingKey: They take in thermal energy from the surroundings; “cold” is not a substance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to Carbon monoxide alarms, explain how it illustrates dangers of incomplete combustion.
items.answer: After many deaths from faulty heaters, many countries now require CO alarms in homes with fuel-burning appliances. Cheap detectors save lives because CO cannot be seen or smelled.
items.markingKey: Context (After many deaths from faulty heaters, many countries now require CO alarms in homes with fuel-burning appliances.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Cheap detectors save lives because CO cannot be seen or smelled. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to dangers of incomplete combustion.

items.stem: Briefly describe Self-heating cans and explain what it reveals about using exothermic reactions.
items.answer: Some cans of coffee have a separate chamber of calcium oxide and water; pressing a button mixes them, an exothermic reaction heats the drink. Useful for campers and emergencies, though the cans are bulky and costly.
items.markingKey: Context (Some cans of coffee have a separate chamber of calcium oxide and water; pressing a button mixes them, an exothermic reaction heats the drink.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Useful for campers and emergencies, though the cans are bulky and costly. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to using exothermic reactions.

items.stem:
Hana measured the volume of hydrogen produced in 1 minute when 0.1 g of magnesium ribbon reacted with hydrochloric acid of different concentrations.

Acid concentration / mol/dm³ | Volume of hydrogen / cm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.25 | 9 | 9 | 8
0.5 | 18 | 18 | 18
0.75 | 27 | 26 | 27
1.0 | 36 | 35 | 36
1.25 | 46 | 45 | 44

Calculate the mean volume of hydrogen when the acid concentration was 0.25 mol/dm³.
items.answer: 8.7 cm³
items.markingKey: M1 (9 + 9 + 8) ÷ 3; A1 8.7 cm³ (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: In an investigation into whether mass is conserved when sodium hydrogencarbonate reacts with vinegar in an open and a sealed container, state the dependent variable and describe how Aiko should measure it.
items.answer: change in total mass measured on a balance (to 0.01 g)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: change in total mass measured on a balance (to 0.01 g).

items.stem: Classify each change as physical or chemical and justify: (a) a candle burning, (b) wax melting, (c) a nail rusting, (d) salt dissolving. Explain why a burning candle involves both.
items.answer: (a) chemical – new substances CO₂, water, soot; irreversible; heat and light. (b) physical – no new substance, reversible on cooling. (c) chemical – iron oxide formed, colour change, irreversible. (d) physical – salt recovered by evaporation. Candle: wax melts (physical) and the vapour burns (chemical).
items.markingKey: (a) chemical – new substances CO₂, water, soot; irreversible; heat and light. (b) physical – no new substance, reversible on cooling. (c) chemical – iron oxide formed, colour change, irreversible. (d) physical – salt recovered by evaporation. Candle: wax melts (physical) and the vapour burns (chemical).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Homes should stop using gas for cooking and heating."
items.answer: Moving away from gas reduces emissions and indoor pollution, especially with renewable electricity, but needs support with costs.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: burning gas releases CO₂ (climate change) and indoor pollutants; risk of CO poisoning and explosions. Arguments against: electric alternatives can be more expensive to install; electricity may also come from fossil fuels. Supported judgement: Moving away from gas reduces emissions and indoor pollution, especially with renewable electricity, but needs support with costs. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Reusable hand warmers are better than single-use ones."
items.answer: Reusable warmers are better for the environment for regular use, though single-use ones suit long trips.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: less waste; cheaper over time. Arguments against: must be reset by boiling, needing energy; single-use types last longer (hours). Supported judgement: Reusable warmers are better for the environment for regular use, though single-use ones suit long trips. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Describe how to use reactions with dilute hydrochloric acid to put four metals (copper, iron, magnesium, zinc) in order of reactivity, including how to make it a fair test and what you expect to see.
items.answer: Same volume and concentration of acid in test tubes; same mass/size and surface area of each metal; same temperature; observe bubbles and measure temperature rise or gas volume in a fixed time. Expect magnesium fastest (vigorous fizz, hot), then zinc, then iron (slow bubbles), copper no reaction. Test gas with lit splint – squeaky pop.
items.markingKey: Same volume and concentration of acid in test tubes; same mass/size and surface area of each metal; same temperature; observe bubbles and measure temperature rise or gas volume in a fixed time. Expect magnesium fastest (vigorous fizz, hot), then zinc, then iron (slow bubbles), copper no reaction. Test gas with lit splint – squeaky pop.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "open system"?
options: A system where gases can escape or enter
The compound formed when a metal reacts with oxygen
A lit splint gives a squeaky pop in hydrogen
The three things needed for burning: fuel, oxygen and heat
items.answer: A system where gases can escape or enter
items.markingKey: A. "open system" is a system where gases can escape or enter.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "chemical change"?
options: A change in which new substances are formed and which is usually hard to reverse
(s), (l), (g) and (aq) showing solid, liquid, gas and aqueous solution
A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen
A device using an exothermic reaction (often iron oxidation) to release heat
items.answer: A change in which new substances are formed and which is usually hard to reverse
items.markingKey: A. "chemical change" is a change in which new substances are formed and which is usually hard to reverse.

items.stem: What are the products of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel?
items.answer: Carbon dioxide and water
items.markingKey: Carbon dioxide and water. Plenty of oxygen.

items.stem: "All reactions that need heating are endothermic." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Many exothermic reactions (e.g. burning) need heat to start; the overall energy change decides the type.
items.markingKey: Many exothermic reactions (e.g. burning) need heat to start; the overall energy change decides the type. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "All metals react with acids to make hydrogen." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Metals below hydrogen in the reactivity series, such as copper, silver and gold, do not react with dilute acids.
items.markingKey: Metals below hydrogen in the reactivity series, such as copper, silver and gold, do not react with dilute acids. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Mass is lost when wood burns because the ash is lighter." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The missing mass is in the gases (CO₂ and water vapour) that escape; including them, mass is conserved.
items.markingKey: The missing mass is in the gases (CO₂ and water vapour) that escape; including them, mass is conserved. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why dissolving salt in water is a physical change.
items.answer: No new substance is made; the salt can be recovered by evaporating the water.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: No new substance is made; the salt can be recovered by evaporating the water. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between incomplete combustion and complete combustion.
items.answer: Complete combustion has plenty of oxygen and produces CO₂ and water with a blue flame; incomplete combustion has limited oxygen and produces carbon monoxide and soot with a yellow, smoky flame.
items.markingKey: Complete combustion has plenty of oxygen and produces CO₂ and water with a blue flame; incomplete combustion has limited oxygen and produces carbon monoxide and soot with a yellow, smoky flame. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Endothermic reactions make things colder because they produce cold." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: They take in thermal energy from the surroundings; “cold” is not a substance.
items.markingKey: They take in thermal energy from the surroundings; “cold” is not a substance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the reactivity of a metal affects the temperature rise when it reacts with hydrochloric acid, state the dependent variable and describe how Mohammed should measure it.
items.answer: temperature rise of the acid in 2 minutes
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: temperature rise of the acid in 2 minutes.

items.stem: Using Antoine Lavoisier (1770s) as an example, explain law of conservation of mass.
items.answer: Lavoisier carefully weighed reactants and products in sealed vessels and showed that mass is conserved; he also showed that burning is a reaction with oxygen. His careful measurements helped turn chemistry into a quantitative science.
items.markingKey: Context (Lavoisier carefully weighed reactants and products in sealed vessels and showed that mass is conserved; he also showed that burning is a reaction with oxygen.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: His careful measurements helped turn chemistry into a quantitative science. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to law of conservation of mass.

items.stem:
Isabel measured the temperature change when different masses of magnesium powder were added to 25 cm³ of acid.

Mass of magnesium / g | Temperature rise / °C: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.1 | 3.5 | 3.5 | 3.3
0.2 | 7.0 | 6.5 | 6.7
0.3 | 10.2 | 10.0 | 10.4
0.4 | 13.1 | 13.4 | 13.7
0.5 | 17.2 | 16.2 | 16.5

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The temperature rise increases in proportion to the mass of magnesium added. The reaction releases energy; more magnesium reacting releases more energy, warming the acid more.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The temperature rise increases in proportion to the mass of magnesium added.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: The reaction releases energy; more magnesium reacting releases more energy, warming the acid more.

items.stem: Maya plans to investigate how the type of metal carbonate affects how quickly it thermally decomposes. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: mass of carbonate (1 g); volume of limewater (5 cm³); Bunsen flame (blue, same height); the same tubes and delivery tube
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: mass of carbonate (1 g) – more carbonate gives more gas; volume of limewater (5 cm³) – more limewater takes longer to go cloudy; Bunsen flame (blue, same height) – heat input affects rate; the same tubes and delivery tube – gas must travel the same path. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: Mohammed wants to find out how the mass of ammonium nitrate dissolved affects the temperature drop of the water. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does mass of ammonium nitrate affect temperature drop?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (mass of ammonium nitrate (1, 2, 3, 4, 5 g)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (temperature drop measured with a thermometer) in a question form.

items.stem:
Tomás measured the volume of hydrogen produced in 1 minute when 0.1 g of magnesium ribbon reacted with hydrochloric acid of different concentrations.

Acid concentration / mol/dm³ | Volume of hydrogen / cm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.25 | 9 | 9 | 9
0.5 | 18 | 18 | 18
0.75 | 27 | 26 | 27
1.0 | 36 | 37 | 37
1.25 | 43 | 44 | 43

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The volume of hydrogen produced in 1 minute increases as acid concentration increases. More concentrated acid has more acid particles in the same volume, so they collide with the magnesium more often and the reaction is faster.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The volume of hydrogen produced in 1 minute increases as acid concentration increases.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: More concentrated acid has more acid particles in the same volume, so they collide with the magnesium more often and the reaction is faster.

items.stem: 2.4 g of magnesium burns completely to form 4 g of magnesium oxide. Calculate the mass of oxygen that reacted.
items.markingKey: M1 mass of oxygen = mass of oxide − mass of magnesium = 4 − 2.4; A1 1.6 g.

items.stem: Chloé investigated how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the time for a marble chip to stop fizzing. The method had this weakness: marble chips were different sizes. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: weigh chips and choose ones of similar mass and size, or use powder of a fixed mass
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: weigh chips and choose ones of similar mass and size, or use powder of a fixed mass

items.stem: "Coating steel with zinc is the best way to prevent bridges from rusting." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Galvanising is excellent for many steel parts but engineers compare costs and conditions to choose the best protection.
